title: Review: Evolution
author: John Kendall Hawkins
content:
Once upon a time, anthropologists and archaeologists told us that Lucy was the
bridge to our ancient common past with monkey people. Very controversial.
Hopelessly irresponsible mainstream media showed us an artist's rendition of a
female bone of contention. Dog mats everywhere howled their disapproval. I
myself formed my own image of what she would look like today. I went with
Scarlett Johansson. Check it out and tell me I'm wrong:

No way, the critics scolded, conjuring up pictures of Imogene Coco in the hit
60s TV series It's About Time.

I don't know. The Hall Lucy phenomenon didn't seem to last very long. The
Bridging Ape Woman made the cover of Time magazine. And for a while, talking
heads contended on air, lightweights self-stimming, while hanky panky (Prince
Bandar reference to hanky panky in Eden as a rationale for corruption now) was
going on behind the scenes, we later learned. Then they release the greatest
hits of Donald J Trump, including the number one hit: they let you touch their
pussies and anything.

Well, the BBC has a new five-part science series out titled Evolution. The
wits and scribes are already comparing it to the best of David Attenborough.
So that seemed like a good enough reason to give it a view. You can't get the
program directly online where I am because the UK government will lock you
out. You have to use a VPN. More importantly, you have to make up an address
in the UK and affirm that you paid the tax on watching TV. Being an American
familiar with the history of outrageous British taxes (and I say there's
drinking tea right now) I was quite fine with dodging requirements, and the
steps to do so were abundantly available on the internet. Honestly, you could
see why George Orwell would have set 1984 in the UK.

(As an aside, things are so intrusively internet of everything right now, so
full with ultra surveillance sensors everywhere, I expect to see any day now
the remaining lefties from the 60s going around the CBD with rat cages on
their faces and sneering two plus two equals four, the rats getting hungrier.)

But seriously why does Donald J Trump keep telling us He fears that the
Iranians will decapitate him, as if we should feel sorry for our bleegory
leader, m*********** goes and carpet bombs more civilian infrastructure the
next day? And how much is he or his family making on side bets every time he
calls off a ceasefire in the gulf.

Anywhere the new series does look worth watching. Replacing Attenborough (as
if) is new guy X. Attenborough went to a good school, and his language skills
were highly polished, like his teeth. The new guys from Liverpool, it sounds
like you may have hung out at the bad cave that The Beatles started out in and
Liverpool. Plus I thought I saw a tooth that was very British working class.
But that aside the guy sure seemed to know his stuff.

As I've mentioned the series is broken up in the five parts and the way x has
decided to do this was to give us five iconic animals and trace their genetic
mapping back to the beginning now they got to where they are today. The five
animals he chose are elephants, bats, …..

This case study method is very effective for a short series as it allows the
narrator to tell the story and plunge its depths, while also giving him a
concrete present example of how it all works. The narrator begins by telling
us what we can expect to learn in the series, just as Lord Attenborough used
to do.

The narrator begins episode 1 by telling us that all life forms trace back to
a tiny entity called LUCA, the Last Unified Common Ancestor of us all—fauna
and flora. The whole big shebang. What is struck with all for a moment, which
is about all the attention span any of us has left. Lucy was just bone p***
compared to Luca.

More on the nuts of bolts of LUCA.

We begin by examining the strange and wonderful evolutionary development of
the elephant. X goes….

He spends a lot of time on the nose of the pachyderm. More details, including
visuals and descriptions of the elephant’s tiny distant relative….

Somewhere in all of this narration, I begin to see a pattern emerging of the
narrator trying to find his niche as a documentarian. X has the side of that
he's going to tell a lot of puns. Give examples of some puns. This is lame but
endearing as he seems to be trying to Molly cuddle theory ship who don't mind
blame but endearing concepts. -- like democracy and the 21st century.

I myself remember elephants well. Well, not really. Australian university, I
was an anthropology major, and one of the first things I had to read was The
Forest People, which depicted the Mbuti pygmies of the Ituri Forest. Real
socialists, you had to admire the way they clanned together, gladly fostering
each other's kids (I enviously compared how those Mbuti kids were treated
compared to my own unwelcome stints in foster care, where the Father's belt
came off too often and too easily over what some minor sarcasm). The Mbuti
moved around everywhere with the elephants and thrived, until the hunters came
looking for tusks, devastating the herds so some Hemingway hero could furnish
ivory for the Steinway piano keyboard industry. Now the Mbuti all f***** up,
fighting over remaining elephants, if there are even any left, and with the
game so bad on the poaching front that keyboards have plastic keys now.
F******. Like Dylan asked all those years ago, who's going to take away their
license to kill?

It's hard to believe I come from the same stock as he's right-wing not jobs
who are living entities brought into this world for one function and one
function only to kill life. Have a think on that paradox and then pass the
bong.

Episodes 2-5 look like they will be excellent too. Here’s a short summary of
each episode and its precious thesis.

Concluding paragraph that has won as John Hurt playing The Elephant Man. I am
not an animal I'm a human being. We cry. And then they shoot him down. Tsk,
tsk.

No doubt someone will make a lot of Lucre off of LUCA. T-shirts will abound.
Contention will be all around us. We will puke himself disgust as we think of
what they do with abattoirs -- chickum, lambs, cows, and even kangaroos. Will
get sick every time we feel the need to mow the lawn. Eventually tension will
pass and we'll note that the. Mountainous surplus of LUCA t-shirts will go the
way of Che and end up delivered by cargo ship to the colorful people of Papua
New Guinea. The gods _must_ be crazy.
